newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major seeks to defuse sleaze row.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major seeks to defuse sleaze row.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major tried on Monday to defuse the row over sleaze that has dogged his party for the first two weeks of his campaign for Britain's May 1 election.

With two politicians from his Conservative Party resisting pressure to resign over allegations of impropriety, Major wrote to local party officials warning that he would act "quickly and decisively" against any MP found guilty of wrongdoing.
Ten Conservative MPs are under investigation by a parliamentary committee into allegations that they accepted payments in exchange for asking questions in the House of Commons (lower house.)
One Conservative MP resigned last week over the allegations and another two have stepped down because of scandal in their private lives.

But Neil Hamilton, accused of accepting hefty payments from Harrods owner Mohammed Al-Fayed, and Piers Merchant, a married MP alleged to have had a too-public fling with a 17-year-old night-club hostess, have defied resignation calls from senior party figures.

The committee's report into the "cash for questions" affair will not be published until after the election and opposition Labour has accused Major of closing parliament early to avoid its findings being made public before polling day.
But Major said in his letter that he would support tough action against any MPs criticised in the report.
He said local Conservative party groups were free to choose their own candidates, but that the day of reckoning would come after the election.
"The House of Commons has draconian powers. The Conservative Party will support their use if criticism is severe enough to merit it," he wrote.
The prime minister appeared to have shifted from recent remarks in which he urged the resignations of Hamilton and Merchant, both of whom have the support of their local parties.
The sleaze issue has given Labour an unexpected boost in the early stages of the election campaign.
The opposition party has a lead of over 20 points over the Conservatives and this has recently risen as high as 28 points.
But Labour leader Tony Blair said on Monday he wanted to rise above sleaze and turn the focus of the campaign to policy.
"I do not want this election fought on negative issues. I want it fought on the policies that we offer to the people of our country," he told supporters.
Nevertheless, a statement issued by his deputy, John Prescott, made clear that the opposition was not quite ready to drop the sleaze issue.

"If Mr Major thinks that this letter draws a line under the issue he is wrong. While he fails to give leadership, sleaze will continue to dominate this election because the state of the Tory (Conservative) party and the weakness of John Major are of vital importance to everyone casting a vote on May 1," Prescott said.
While leading Conservatives took a day's rest on Monday, a national holiday in Britain, Blair was on the campaign trail, outlining his party's policies.
He said Labour would divert 100 million pounds ($160 million) in the national health service from administration costs to patient care.
He promised safer streets, smaller classes in schools, low interest and mortgage rates and no income tax increases for the life of the next parliament.
